title: Six of ten CTO-level leaders Gergely Orosz canvassed are leaving or taking a career break, and the reasons they give are mostly about AI
summary: Gergely Orosz spoke with almost twenty CTOs, VPs of Engineering and Heads of Engineering who are on a career break or seriously considering one, after a Bay Area head of engineering told him that two of the four startups he was interviewing with had lost their founding engineering leader to a full break. Among the CTO-level people Orosz then asked privately, six of ten said they are on the way out. The reasons he groups are specific and mostly AI-shaped: boards and founders expecting the CTO to make the company 'AI-native' while also cutting engineering costs 20-50%; founders going hands-on and shipping what one CTO called 'founder slop' — the example given is a founder merging a 60,000-line pull request 'gleaming with joy at how much more productive they've become'; smaller teams meaning less need for leaders; and AI startups paying individual contributors more than non-AI startups pay executives. Two structural reasons are not about AI capability at all but about AI's effect on company value: leaders judging that their equity sits behind a preference stack their company will never clear, and leaders concluding they are not AI-native enough for their other skills to stay marketable. This is a canvass, not a survey, and Orosz says plainly that he has not seen this many capable engineering leaders opt out in twenty years in the industry.
sampleSize: almost 20 engineering leaders on or considering a career break, canvassed privately; of ten CTO-level people asked directly, six said they are leaving. Named on-record contributors include Charity Majors, Claire Vo, Karthik Hariharan, Katelyn Lesse and Matt Boyle; the quoted departing CTOs and VPEs are anonymous.
leadTimeEstimate: ~9-18 months ahead of it showing up in executive-tenure data or recruiter reporting
whyItMatters: The engineering leadership layer is where an AI transformation is actually executed. If the people asked to run it are the ones leaving, a board that has mandated 'AI-native by next year' is losing the only role that can deliver it.

The mechanism named most often is not overwork but a mandate contradiction: transform the company with AI while cutting 20-50% of engineering cost. That is a brief a board can withdraw or rewrite, unlike burnout, which is usually treated as the individual's problem.

'Founder slop' names a governance gap that is new: when a founder or CEO ships code directly, the accountability rules of you-build-it-you-own-it do not resolve who is on call for it, and the CTO has no standing to refuse the merge.

Two of the ten reasons are financial rather than operational — worthless equity behind a preference stack, and AI startups paying ICs more than executives elsewhere. Retention packages aimed at workload will not touch either.
recommendedActions: Write down the engineering leader's mandate explicitly and check it for contradiction: an AI-native transformation target and a 20-50% cost-reduction target in the same year is the pattern these leaders describe leaving over.

Set an accountability rule for founder- and executive-authored code before it becomes an incident: who reviews it, who is on call for it, and whether it can bypass the standards everyone else follows.
For Director+ retention, check whether the equity is actually reachable given the preference stack, rather than assuming the grant size is doing the retaining.
risksAndCaveats: This is a self-selected canvass by a journalist, not a survey. There is no denominator, no sampling frame, and the '6 of 10' is from people Orosz chose to ask because he suspected the pattern.
The most damaging quotes are anonymous, so neither the companies nor the claims can be independently checked.

Executive churn at startups is high in every cycle, and this article cannot separate an AI-specific effect from a downturn in venture funding — the equity and growth reasons it gives would apply with no AI at all.
The source is paywalled, which limits independent verification by readers.
Career-break trends are visible early in networks like this one and can fail to appear in population-level data at all.
